purpose: Specify negative test cases for escrow settlement (role-based access control, mutual exclusivity, amount conservation)

testCases.name: Release Path with Wrong Buyer Key
testCases.description: Attempt escrow release using a key that is NOT the registered buyer
testCases.precondition: Escrow covenant with buyer=BUYER_KEY, seller=SELLER_KEY, arbiter=ARBITER_KEY
testCases.action: Call release path with signature from attacker_key (not BUYER_KEY)
testCases.expectedBehavior: rejected by covenant script (signature verification fails)
testCases.why: Covenant enforces role-based access; only buyer can trigger release

testCases.name: Refund Path with Wrong Arbiter Key
testCases.description: Attempt escrow refund using a key that is NOT the registered arbiter
testCases.action: Call refund path with signature from attacker_key (not ARBITER_KEY)
testCases.expectedBehavior: rejected by covenant script (signature verification fails)
testCases.why: Only arbiter can trigger refund; prevents buyer from self-refunding or seller from blocking refund

testCases.name: Cancel Path with Wrong Seller Key
testCases.description: Attempt escrow cancel using a key that is NOT the registered seller
testCases.action: Call cancel path with signature from attacker_key (not SELLER_KEY)
testCases.expectedBehavior: rejected by covenant script (signature verification fails)
testCases.why: Only seller can cancel; prevents buyer from canceling and getting refund without consent

testCases.name: Release to Wrong Recipient Address
testCases.description: Buyer attempts to release funds to address other than registered seller
testCases.action: Call release path with output going to attacker_address instead of SELLER_ADDRESS
testCases.expectedBehavior: rejected by covenant script (output constraint violation)
testCases.why: Covenant locks output recipient to seller; prevents buyer from stealing funds by redirecting release

testCases.name: Refund to Wrong Recipient Address
testCases.description: Arbiter attempts to refund to address other than original buyer
testCases.action: Call refund path with output going to attacker_address instead of BUYER_ADDRESS
testCases.expectedBehavior: rejected by covenant script (output constraint violation)
testCases.why: Covenant locks refund recipient to buyer; prevents arbiter from stealing funds

testCases.name: Replay Attack (Spend Same Input Twice)
testCases.description: After escrow release is confirmed, attacker replays the same transaction to spend the UTXO again
testCases.precondition: Escrow release transaction broadcast and accepted on-chain
testCases.action: Submit identical release transaction with same input (UTXO already spent)
testCases.expectedBehavior: rejected by mempool (input already spent) or by chain (orphan UTXO)
testCases.why: Escrow covenant prevents replay by consuming the UTXO; once released, cannot release again

testCases.name: Release with Amount Greater Than Input
testCases.description: Attempt to release more funds than escrow contract holds
testCases.precondition: Escrow holds 100 TKAS; attempt to release with output = 101 TKAS
testCases.action: Build release transaction with output amount > input amount (violates conservation law)
testCases.expectedBehavior: rejected by covenant (or by transaction builder due to insufficient input)
testCases.why: Cannot create funds out of thin air; covenant enforces amount conservation

testCases.name: Release with Zero Fee (Dust Output)
testCases.description: Attempt to release with fee so high that output becomes dust (< 546 satoshis)
testCases.precondition: Escrow holds 100 satoshi, fee = 100 satoshi → output = 0
testCases.action: Build release with excessive fee, creating zero-value output
testCases.expectedBehavior: rejected by covenant or transaction validator (zero output disallowed)
testCases.why: Standard validation rules reject zero outputs; prevents fund destruction

testCases.name: Multiple Settlement Paths in Same Transaction
testCases.description: Attempt to include both release AND refund in same transaction
testCases.precondition: Escrow contract with distinct release and refund code paths
testCases.action: Build transaction that satisfies both release and refund witness constraints
testCases.expectedBehavior: rejected by covenant (mutual exclusivity enforced in script logic)
testCases.why: Covenant enforces exactly one settlement path; prevents double-spending in same block

testCases.name: Release After Seller Cancels
testCases.description: Seller cancels escrow (resetting state), then buyer tries to release
testCases.precondition: Escrow has expiry; seller calls cancel, which expires the escrow state
testCases.action: After cancel, attempt to call release path using original buyer key
testCases.expectedBehavior: rejected by covenant (escrow state invalid or expired after cancel)
testCases.why: Covenant tracks expiry/state; settlement impossible after cancel

testCases.name: Malleated Signature (Flip S Value)
testCases.description: Attacker modifies valid signature by flipping the S value in ECDSA (low_s vs high_s)
testCases.precondition: Valid buyer signature on release path
testCases.action: Flip S value (S → order - S) while keeping rest of signature same
testCases.expectedBehavior: rejected by covenant if using strict DER-encoded signatures
testCases.why: Standard script validation enforces signature canonicality; prevents signature malleability attacks

testCases.name: Release with Missing Witness Data
testCases.description: Attempt release without providing buyer signature in witness
testCases.precondition: Escrow release path expects buyer signature
testCases.action: Build transaction without witness data (empty scriptSig)
testCases.expectedBehavior: rejected by covenant script (signature verification fails)
testCases.why: Covenant requires all required signatures; missing signature fails validation

executionStrategy.successCriteria: All 12 cases correctly rejected; all 3 legitimate paths (release, refund, cancel) still work

implementationNotes: Escrow negative tests focus on role-based access control (RBAC) enforcement and mutual exclusivity. Most critical failures are key/signature mismatches (attacker uses wrong key). Amount conservation and output constraints are secondary validations.
